title: Butch O'Hare's last flight

facts.text: On the night of 26 November 1943, Lieutenant Commander Edward "Butch" O'Hare, commander of the air group on USS Enterprise, led the U.S. Navy's first night fighter attack ever launched from an aircraft carrier.

The stakes were the carriers off the Gilbert Islands. Japanese Betty bombers from the Marshall Islands were hunting them with torpedoes, and two days earlier, on 24 November, a submarine torpedo had blown up the escort carrier Liscome Bay with the loss of more than six hundred men.

O'Hare's team was two Hellcat fighters and one radar equipped Avenger torpedo plane: O'Hare and Ensign Warren "Andy" Skon in the Hellcats, and Lieutenant Commander John Phillips flying the Avenger, with Hazen Rand on the radar and Alvin Kernan in the rear turret.
O'Hare took off at about 6 p.m. in F6F Hellcat Bureau No. 66168. Rand's radar led them to a formation of Bettys, and Kernan's fire set one bomber's wing tanks ablaze and sent it into the sea.
When Phillips switched on his running lights so the fighters could form up, a Betty slipped in among them behind O'Hare. Phillips radioed a warning and Kernan fired at the bomber, which fired back.

Skon reported: "I saw Mr O'Hare's lights go out and, at the same instant, he seemed to veer off and slant down into darkness." O'Hare's plane was never found. He was listed as missing and declared dead a year later.

For decades the usual story was that friendly fire from the Avenger killed him, based on a 1962 history of Enterprise. A 1997 study by Steve Ewing and John Lundstrom concluded that the Betty's nose gunner most likely shot him down and that Kernan had been wrongly blamed.

O'Hare was already famous. On 20 February 1942, defending USS Lexington, he attacked a formation of Betty bombers alone after his wingman's guns jammed. He was credited with five, though the records show three, and became the Navy's first ace of the war.
On 21 April 1942 President Roosevelt presented him the Medal of Honor at the White House, the first awarded to a naval aviator in the war.
His name outlived the war: on 19 September 1949 the city's Orchard Field was renamed O'Hare International Airport in his honor. The Navy also named a destroyer, USS O'Hare, for him.

The film shows O'Hare's own Wildcat of Fighting Squadron 3, marked F-13, flying with his commander John Thach's F-1 near Kaneohe, Oahu. A Navy photographer took a still of the same two planes on 10 April 1942.

photoNote: Tier: green. Two F4F-3 Wildcats of VF-3 near NAS Kaneohe, Oahu, 10 April 1942: BuNo 3976 (F-1, foreground) flown by Lt Cdr John Thach and BuNo 3986 (F-13, behind) flown by Lt Edward O'Hare. Photo by PhoM2c H.S. Fawcett, U.S. Navy, NHHC 80-G-10613, public domain (Commons original 5681 x 4369; saved 1920 x 1477). Not the night of 26 Nov 1943: it is O'Hare's plane in 1942, so caption it so. Chosen because every public domain face photo of O'Hare on Commons is under 800 px (portrait in F4F cockpit with five flags, 694 x 555, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Butch_O%27Hare.jpg; standing in cockpit 10 Apr 1942, 80-G-10562, 595 x 765). Runner up for faces: NARA 80-G-63833, "Lieut. Edward H. O'Hare, USN, VF-3", 10 April 1942 (naId 221949809), not digitized online; Brian could order a scan if he wants a face. The Wildcats match the noon film (same flight).
photoCredit: Butch O'Hare's Wildcat (F-13, rear) flying with John Thach's F-1 near Kaneohe, Oahu, 10 April 1942. U.S. Navy photo, NHHC 80-G-10613, public domain.

declassified.fact: The turret gunner who fired at the Betty that night, Alvin Kernan, came home and became a leading Shakespeare scholar, a dean at Yale and then of Princeton's Graduate School. He wrote his own account of O'Hare's last flight and died in 2018 at 94.

film.shot_notes: Whole Navy reel, 10 min 38 s, 720 x 480, silent (track is near silence). 00:00 to 00:12 slate. 00:15 to 01:30 two pilots study a chart beside a Wildcat (unidentified, likely Thach and O'Hare; do not name them). 01:30 to 03:00 pilots climb in, cockpit close ups 01:55 to 02:15 and 02:45 to 03:00. 03:05 to 03:35 F-1 airborne over cloud. 03:50 to 05:25 close air to air of F-1 and a wingman. 05:30 to 05:50 O'Hare's F-13 banks in close, the number clear at 05:35 to 05:45: best opening. 05:50 to 08:20 mock dogfight, planes small against cloud (weaker). 08:20 to 08:40 F-13 again. 09:10 to 10:00 close formation. 10:05 end card. NOON: open on F-13 at 05:33, then 03:05 to 03:35 and 05:00 to 05:30. If a second cut is ever needed: 01:55 to 03:00 cockpits, 03:50 to 04:55, 09:10 to 10:00.
film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (U.S. Navy, NARA Record Group 428). NARA use status 'Undetermined', the routine flag on 428-NPC reels.
film.date_note: Not filmed on 26 Nov 1943. The reel is VF-3 over Oahu in spring 1942 (NARA gives no date; F-1 and F-13 match NHHC photo 80-G-10613 of 10 April 1942). Caption it as O'Hare's Wildcat in 1942; there is no film of the night action.

video.note: U.S. Navy film 428-NPC-16144, Activities of Fighter Squadron 3 (NARA 80315), VF-3 over Oahu in spring 1942, silent; not film of 26 November 1943. Cut 19 Nov 2026 from footage/1943-11-26-ohare-vf3.mp4: 5:33.0 to 5:41.0 O'Hare's Wildcat F-13 banking in close, the number clear; 3:07.5 to 3:11.5 Thach's F-1 over the clouds; 5:12.0 to 5:16.0 F-1 with a wingman. The pilots studying a chart (unidentified) are left out. Converted to square pixels.

body:
In the dark off the Gilberts, a Japanese bomber slipped in among three American planes. One of them was flown by Butch O'Hare, and it was never found.

26 November 1943. O'Hare, commander of the air group on USS Enterprise, was leading the first night fighter attack the Navy had ever launched from a carrier. Betty bombers were hunting the carriers off the Gilbert Islands, and two days earlier a submarine had blown up the escort carrier Liscome Bay with more than six hundred men.

His team was two Hellcats and one radar Avenger. Hazen Rand's radar found the bombers, and gunner Alvin Kernan set one on fire. When the Avenger switched on its running lights so the fighters could form up, a Betty crept in behind O'Hare.

Ensign Andy Skon saw O'Hare's lights go out as his Hellcat slanted down into the darkness.

For decades Kernan was blamed. A 1997 study concluded the Betty's nose gunner most likely fired the fatal shots.

O'Hare had already received the Medal of Honor, for taking on a formation of bombers alone to defend USS Lexington in 1942. In 1949 Chicago's Orchard Field became O'Hare International Airport.
